title: Diffie-Hellman Key Agreement Method
summary: Standardizes one variant of Diffie-Hellman key agreement, based on a draft from the ANSI X9F1 working group. Two parties can use it to arrive at a shared secret over an open channel.

plainLanguage.summary: Diffie-Hellman lets two computers work out the same secret without ever sending it across the network. RFC 2631 pins down one standard way to do it and explains how to turn the result into keys. The whole scheme depends on each side keeping its private key secret.

how is a kek derived from diffie-hellman
what is the zz value in diffie-hellman
subtitle: How two parties use Diffie-Hellman to agree on a secret over an open channel, and turn it into usable keys.

tldr.problem: Two parties that have never shared a secret need to agree on one over an open channel, and the many slightly different Diffie-Hellman variants made implementations disagree.
tldr.mechanism: Each side combines its own private key with the other party's public key to compute the same shared number, called ZZ. A SHA-1 based function then turns ZZ plus some context into as much keying material as needed, typically a key-encryption key.
tldr.outcome: Ephemeral-Static mode MUST be implemented and Static-Static mode is optional. All the security rests on keeping private keys secret, and static keys need protection against small subgroup attacks.

today: RFC 2631 is a Proposed Standard published in June 1999, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It remains the standard form of Diffie-Hellman key agreement for use with the Cryptographic Message Syntax.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2631 standardizes one particular variant of the Diffie-Hellman key agreement algorithm, based on the ANSI X9.42 draft developed by the ANSI X9F1 working group. Diffie-Hellman lets two parties agree on a shared secret in such a way that the secret is unavailable to eavesdroppers.

The secret can then be converted into keying material for other, symmetric algorithms. A large number of minor variants of the process exist, and this document describes one of them. The variant requires the recipient to have a certificate, while the originator may have a static key pair, with its public key placed in a certificate, or an ephemeral key pair.
sections.plainLanguage: Two computers can agree on a secret number that nobody listening in can work out. This RFC picks one standard way of doing that, so different implementations still end up with the same answer.

sections.title: Overview of the Method
sections.content:
Key agreement requires that both the sender and the recipient of a message have key pairs. By combining one's own private key with the other party's public key, both parties compute the same shared secret number. That number is then converted into cryptographic keying material.

The keying material is typically used as a key-encryption key (KEK) to wrap a content-encryption key (CEK), and the CEK is what encrypts the message data. The first stage of the process is to compute a shared secret number called ZZ. The same ZZ value results whenever the same originator and recipient key pairs are used. When the originator employs a static private and public key pair, the introduction of a public random value ensures that the resulting symmetric key is different for each key agreement.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side mixes its own secret key with the other side's public key. Both sides get the same number, which becomes the key used to protect the message. A random value added to the mix means the key changes every time.

sections.title: Generating the Shared Secret ZZ
sections.content:
The shared secret is generated as ZZ = g ^ (xb * xa) mod p. The individual parties actually perform the computations ZZ = (yb ^ xa) mod p = (ya ^ xb) mod p, where ^ denotes exponentiation.

Here ya is party A's public key and xb is party B's private key, and the other symbols follow the same pattern. The value p is a large prime, q is a large prime, j is a large integer such that p = qj + 1, and g = h^((p-1)/q) mod p, where h is any integer with 1 < h < p-1 such that h^((p-1)/q) mod p > 1. The generator g has order q modulo p.

In CMS the recipient's key is identified by the CMS RecipientIdentifier, which points to the recipient's certificate. The sender's public key is identified using the OriginatorIdentifierOrKey field, either by reference to the sender's certificate or by inline inclusion of a public key.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side raises the other side's public number to the power of its own secret number, using a big prime modulus. Both sides reach the same answer without ever transmitting it.

sections.title: Generating Keying Material
sections.content:
The keying material comes from KM = H(ZZ || OtherInfo), where H is the SHA-1 message digest function. Leading zeros MUST be preserved so that ZZ occupies as many octets as p; for instance, if p is 1024 bits, ZZ should be 128 bytes long.

OtherInfo is the DER encoding of a structure holding a KeySpecificInfo with the algorithm object identifier of the CEK wrapping algorithm and a counter, an optional partyAInfo and a suppPubInfo field. The counter is a 32-bit number in network byte order whose initial value is 1 for any ZZ, and it is incremented by one every time the key generation function runs for a given KEK. If partyAInfo is provided it MUST contain 512 bits, and suppPubInfo is the length of the generated KEK in bits, represented as a 32-bit number in network byte order.

To generate a KEK, one or more KM blocks are produced, incrementing the counter appropriately, and they are concatenated left to right. The only source of secret entropy in this computation is ZZ, so even a longer output has an effective key space limited by the size of ZZ and by the security level of the parameters p and q. If partyAInfo is different for each message, a different KEK is generated for each message. partyAInfo MUST be used in Static-Static mode but MAY appear in Ephemeral-Static mode.
sections.plainLanguage: The shared number on its own is not a usable key, so it is run through a hash function together with some context. That context includes a counter starting at 1 and going up by one for each key generated, plus the length of key wanted.

sections.title: Key and Parameter Requirements
sections.content:
The group parameters must be of the form p = jq + 1, where q is a large prime of length m and j is at least 2. The private key x must be in the interval [2, q-2] and should be randomly generated in that interval; the public key is then y = g^x mod p.

To comply with this RFC, m MUST be at least 160 bits in length, and consequently q MUST be at least 160 bits long. When symmetric ciphers stronger than DES are to be used, a larger m may be advisable. The prime p must be a minimum of 512 bits long.

Agents SHOULD generate the domain parameters g, p and q using the algorithm given in the RFC, which is derived from FIPS PUB 186 and the ANSI X9.42 draft. When that algorithm is used, the correctness of the generation procedure can be verified by a third party. Two checks are possible: verify that p = qj + 1, which shows the parameters meet the X9.42 criteria, and verify that following the generation procedure with the published seed finds p at the published counter, which shows the parameters were randomly chosen and do not have a special form. Whether agents provide validation information in their certificates is a local matter between the agents and their certification authority.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC sets a floor on the size of the numbers involved: the subgroup prime at least 160 bits and the main prime at least 512 bits. Larger sizes are advisable when the cipher behind them is stronger than DES.

sections.title: Modes and Public Key Validation
sections.content:
A received public key y may be checked with a two-step procedure. First verify that y lies within the interval [2, p-1]; if it does not, the key is invalid. Then compute y^q mod p: if the result is 1 the key is valid, otherwise it is invalid. The primary purpose of public key validation is to prevent a small subgroup attack on the sender's key pair. If Ephemeral-Static mode is used, this check may not be necessary. The RFC notes that the procedure may be subject to pending patents.

In Ephemeral-Static mode the recipient has a static, certified key pair, but the sender generates a new key pair for each message and sends it using the originatorKey production. Because the sender's key is freshly generated for each message, ZZ is different for each message and partyAInfo MAY be omitted. If the same ephemeral sender key is used for multiple messages, for example because it is cached as a performance optimization, a separate partyAInfo MUST be used for each message. All implementations of this standard MUST implement Ephemeral-Static mode, and the recipient SHOULD perform the public key check to resist small subgroup attacks.

In Static-Static mode both the sender and the recipient have static, certified key pairs, so ZZ is the same for every message. partyAInfo MUST then be used, and be different for each message, so that different messages use different KEKs. Implementations MAY implement Static-Static mode, and both originator and recipient SHOULD either perform the validation step or verify that the certification authority has properly verified the key.
sections.plainLanguage: Two modes are defined. In one, the sender picks a fresh key for every message and only the receiver holds a long-term key. In the other, both sides hold long-term keys, so the sender adds a fresh random value to keep each message's key different.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All the security in this system is provided by the secrecy of the private keying material. If either sender or recipient private keys are disclosed, all messages sent or received using that key are compromised. Likewise, loss of the private key results in an inability to read messages sent using that key.

Static Diffie-Hellman keys are vulnerable to a small subgroup attack. In practice this issue arises for both sides in Static-Static mode and for the receiver during Ephemeral-Static mode, and the RFC describes appropriate practices to protect against it.

The security level provided by these methods depends on several factors. It depends on the length of the symmetric key, typically a 2^l security level if the length is l bits; on the size of the prime q, which gives a 2^(m/2) security level; and on the size of the prime p, where the security level grows as a subexponential function of the size in bits. A good design principle is to have a balanced system, where all three security levels are approximately the same. In any case, the overall security is limited by the lowest of the three levels.
sections.plainLanguage: The scheme is only as safe as the private keys, so if one leaks, everything sent with it is exposed. Its strength also depends on three sizes at once, and the weakest of the three sets the ceiling.

viz.caption: ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT FROM THE RFC: THE TWO PUBLIC VALUES ARE EXCHANGED, THEN BOTH SIDES COMPUTE ZZ

messages.label: PUBLIC VALUE ya = g ^ xa mod p
messages.note: Party A sends its public value, with its certificate or its public key.

messages.label: PUBLIC VALUE yb = g ^ xb mod p
messages.note: Party B replies with its public value. Each side now computes the same ZZ.

viz.caption: THE FORMULAS AS PRINTED IN RFC 2631

data.title: Shared secret and keying material
data.code:
ZZ = g ^ (xb * xa) mod p

ZZ = (yb ^ xa)  mod p  = (ya ^ xb)  mod p

KM = H ( ZZ || OtherInfo)
